Designing artificial networks that mimic the properties of natural ones is an essential yet unresolved issue in neuroscience-inspired computing. In our work, we delve into replicating the neural network of the model organism C. Elegans, whose simple nervous system makes it an ideal candidate to study the dynamics of small neural networks. We train and test various types of artificial networks, including different architectures and learning methods, on a dataset that models the responses of the 294 neurons to 100 million stimuli. Our results indicate that the most successful artificial network in reproducing the responses to individual stimuli and navigating the worm through its environment is a ResNet-style feedforward network with binary weights. However, our findings also suggest that the performance of this network is matched by a simpler artificial system based on threshold logic, which shares striking similarities with biologically relevant properties of the natural network. We demonstrate that this simplified artificial system can be used to explain and replicate the behaviors of the natural system in various environmental conditions and stimulus situations. Furthermore, our work explores the limits of overfitting in these artificial systems, reveals their capacity for generalizing to unfamiliar stimuli, and examines the extent to which their design can be guided by the constraints of analog VLSI electronics. In conclusion, our research identifies artificial networks that effectively mimic the natural network of the C. Elegans, and we believe that this achievement lays the groundwork for addressing more complex engineering and biological challenges. We also contend that the model based on threshold logic holds significant value due to its simplicity, making it easier to implement using analog VLSI electronics. Ultimately, our work brings us closer to being able to understand and program the neural control system of the C. Elegans, whose intricate circuitry poses a challenging puzzle in neuroscience. As our research reveals, the outputs of the model hold "built-in" information about the dynamics of the natural system, enabling us to leverage them for predicting the behaviors of the C. Elegans in various environmental conditions and advancing analog electronics capable of replicating its neural control system. In the longer term, our investigation into the architecture of small neural networks like the C. Elegans is part of a broader effort to design artificial systems that can mimic the properties of the brain's microcircuitry in various species. To conclude, our work represents a significant advancement in our ability to understand and replicate artificial systems that mimic the natural behavior of small neural networks, bringing us one step closer to being able to engineer analog VLSI electronics capable of replicating their neural control system. This paper extends the AIR model to incorporate migration and confining mechanisms using the Fokker-Planck equation with a singular coefficient. Similar to the AIR model, the DOCS model uses a Lagrange multiplier to enforce boundary constraints, but it addresses migration using a profession-specific diffusion coefficient. Our analysis focuses on the DOCS model's equilibrium states and the speed of convergence for spatial and temporal dynamics. Numerical simulations demonstrate the impact of diffusion on spatial equilibrium, while a high value of $\varepsilon$ accelerates the temporal equilibrium's convergence. In confined spaces, the model exhibits a coexistence of stable equilibria when migration is lacking. With increasing diffusion, the region of coexistence expands. Migration influences the temporal order of model behavior, shifting from an early stage of exponential growth to a later stage of logistic decay. Our findings are consistent across various diffusion coefficients. Furthermore, the model shows an interesting inverse relationship between spatial and temporal equilibrium characteristics. In spatial analysis, the size of boundary confining regions shrinks with an increasing diffusion coefficient, but this is compensated for in temporal analysis by a larger region of initial infection. Similarly, the broader initial infection region is accompanied by a smaller final infected population size. Additionally, the model indicates an inversely related time-scale for spatial and temporal dynamics. Finally, the model suggests an inversely related speed of propagation between spatial and temporal dynamics. This inverse relationship is evident in all observed model behaviors. Our analysis for the SIS dynamics is based on the DOCS model, but similar results can be derived for the AIR model. Our work is accompanied by a repository containing the model's implementation, available at https://github.com/Jesus-Cardenas-EG/DOCS_model. To investigate the characteristics of planetary systems comprising compact multi-planet systems, which exhibit orbital resonances in terms of their eigenfunctions and Lyapunov indicators, we examined the orbital architecture of a curated sample comprising 35 systems detected by Kepler. By cross-referencing computational models with observational data, we defined and validated a metric to quantify orbital resonance density within these systems. Subsequently, we analyzed statistical properties of compact systems displaying resonant architecture, which we termed Type I systems, and contrasted them with non-resonant compact systems (Non-R) and all compact systems (All Comp). Notably, the Type I system class exhibited distinct properties in terms of planet size and exoplanet ratio, resulting in the identification of two distinct sub-groups: a subgroup resembling solar system analogs and another resembling a sheared-down planet population. All Comp and Non-R groups differed significantly based on Lyapunov indicators and eigenfunction architecture. Our analysis showed that Type I systems, which possess resonant architecture, display unique properties in terms of planetary evolution, suggesting potential mechanisms governing compact system formation. Furthermore, the distinct characteristics of Type I systems may be attributed to planetary evolution within compact systems. Finally, the study outlines future avenues of investigation into compact system exoplanets, which could offer insights into their evolutionary history and comparative dynamics with solar systems. The current state of formal proof archives has a network structure that is comprised of archived formal proofs, with connections made through shared subproofs. Although a few researchers have studied this structure, their findings are limited, and whether it exhibits characteristics of a scale-free network remains unclear. This study aims to answer this question by examining the collaborative structure of the Sophisticed Formal Proof Archives utility in greater detail, specifically looking at the output of the Isabelle theorem prover. Our findings confirm that the proposed utility outperforms existing mathematical networks in terms of scale-free characteristics. This is an important development, as mathematicians typically do not prioritize scale-free structure when creating mathematical networks, as evidenced by studies such as those shown in Bonneau-Alés and Dubois in 2021 and Alstine and others in 2022. These findings suggest that the SFPAs could potentially reap the benefits associated with scale-free structures, including the strength of linked components and the resistance of the system as a whole. However, this study also uncovers a significant issue regarding false-positives in certain mathematical networks, as seen in the intersection of SFPAs and the Erdos-Rényi model. Our research further investigates whether false-positives can prevent the scale-free characteristic from developing over time in networks under certain conditions. In practical terms, this finding implies that mathematicians might face difficulty achieving a scale-free structure if link formations are dependent on the intensity of mathematical influence, such as the frequency of theorem applications. Nevertheless, this study demonstrates that the scale-free characteristic in proof archives is resilient to certain network disturbances. Moreover, we identify a significant issue regarding influence intensity, as evidenced by the significant variation in node in-degrees of the dependency graph from near-zero to hundreds. This disparity might cause mathematicians to prioritize either quantitative or qualitative methods when evaluating mathematical influence. Finally, this study highlights opportunities for further research by suggesting that the scale-free structure in proof archives could be leveraged to develop automated tools that utilize influence to locate and apply relevant subproofs within a vast repository of archived formal proofs. These opportunities could lead to the discovery of novel mathematical concepts that are currently not part of such repositories. Consequently, this discovery could necessitate the implementation of new mathematical networks, as observed in our case study involving the MathOverflow Q&A forum. The outcome of this research could ultimately contribute to the development of SFPAs as a powerful mathematical discovery platform, as discovered in past instances such as the development of the Calabi metric by Xiuxiong Chen. A novel recommender system based on implicit feedback is presented in this paper, leveraging a probabilistic non-linear model. To address a challenging user-item matrix where ratings are absent but essential for recommendation, the proposed method relies on the Indian buffet process (IBP) to assign approximated features to user and item groups. Building upon this, the derived user and item models incorporate a mixture of linear and non-linear components fueled by compactly represented Gaussian mixtures, thereby enabling complex parameter estimation. Experimental validation on data sets with varying sizes demonstrates that the proposed approach surpasses state-of-the-art models renowned for handling large datasets and provides efficient computation benefits. Specifically, the method outperforms popular implicit feedback models such asbpr, lfactor, and fptl on real-world data sets. Moreover, the method exhibits computation time advantages comparable to lfactor and fptl while greatly surpassing the baseline bpr. A key differentiator of the method lies in the direct integration of Gaussian mixtures, whereas related work relies on clustering, necessitating data partitioning and resulting in computation complexities. Consequently, the method allows for a non-Gaussian feature distribution essential for robust user and item models, thus providing a robust framework for recommender systems. By building upon existing theories of anomalous Hall effects in insulators and metals, as well as unique spin Hall and magnetic Hall effects in 2D systems with linear and planar magnetic dipoles, a comprehensive framework has been established. This framework provides a theoretical basis for novel phenomena such as spontaneous magnetic Hall effects in paired electron systems, the proximity effect at boundaries, and the attenuation of anomalous Hall conductivity in thin films by boundaries. Additionally, a many-electron contribution to Hall conductivity has been identified, which can manifest as a positive or negative Hall conductivity even in the absence of an external magnetic field. This phenomenon is particularly prominent in 2D systems, where it can exhibit a linear temperature dependence. This cycle duration is anticipated to be well within the acceptable range of 5 seconds as established in prehospital emergency settings. Multiple patients can be ventilated simultaneously by modifying the ventilator protocol, which involves setting a fixed inspiratory to total cycle ratio unique to each patient and using a single, time-based flow rate profile. The underlying principle is based on the serpent-shaped layout of arranged fermions, which, when subjected to a two-body interaction, escapes localization and begins a diffusive process in a quasi-two-dimensional system, resembling a Pauli crystal's lattice structure. The proposed model applies ab-initio quantum Monte Carlo methods to study the dynamics of this novel system. The model then analyzes the disordered momentum distribution of single particles within Pauli crystals and the time-dependent behavior of this distribution as the disordered wavepackets coalesce into a diffusive wavepacket. The model further demonstrates that Pauli crystals exhibit Brownian motion of their wavepackets, the superposition of which results in a momentum distribution spanning the entire first Brillouin zone. The double precision binary arithmetic used in modern computers introduces a systematic error in numerical computations, even when using widely accepted and trusted algorithms like Euler's method for solving ordinary differential equations (ODRs). In contrast, the discrete version of the zero-nonlinearity algorithm (DZNN) was found to be a reliable and accurate method for solving ODRs that was initially designed to estimate solution values at any point in the course of integration without requiring any additional data. Although DZNN has some similarities to conventional solving methods like Euler's method, it also exhibits distinct features such as self-consistency, low memory requirements, and the ability to predict unknown solution values at any time without additional computations. Recently discovered expressions have allowed DZNN to be extended for solving ODRs with directed derivatives through a new approach, while also deriving the discrete version of the Laplace transform, which confirms that DZNN is capable of accurately solving ODRs without input data. Additionally, DZNN can produce predictive results for ODRs with directed derivatives without requiring any additional computations. What's more, the discrete version of the Laplace transform based on DZNN implies that DZNN can efficiently be applied to a broad range of initial value problems for which the traditional Laplace transform method is used. Furthermore, it's observed that DZNN successfully eliminates the systematic error of ordinary double precision arithmetic, unlike conventional ODR solving methods such as Euler's method. In this study, the key developments and differences between DZNN and other conventional methods such as Euler's method are examined, while also highlighting the benefits of DZNN in terms of double precision accuracy. Additionally, the study demonstrates that DZNN can be trusted in solving various problems related to directed differential equations and initial value problems for ODRs. As such, it may serve as an alternative algorithm to provide high confidence in numerical results, which is particularly significant for double precision computations in solving differential equation problems. Ultimately, the study presents several future research directions for further developing the DZNN algorithm. The synthetic control method is frequently used in causal inference to estimate the impact of a specific treatment, typically represented by a single aggregate unit. Unbalanced data, characterized by differing observation numbers between the treatment and control units, often complicate the estimation of a fair treatment effect. Researchers have previously addressed this issue using weighted regional characteristics, balanced on observed variables, to create a control profile for the treated unit. Existing methods, however, either overlook unbalanced data or ignore the treated unit's data. Developing an estimation process for the weights associated with these controls is challenging due to the difficulty in ensuring the small sample size of control units doesn't adversely affect the weight calculations. To tackle this problem, the authors propose a new approach: the Control Selection, Estimation, and Weighting (CSEW) method. CSEW begins by identifying control units with the most predictive power for the treated unit, using a novel control evaluation metric that accounts for potentially uneven data distribution. These controllable units are then used to estimate weights through weighted average projections. Notably, CSEW can also utilize non-usable control units with damaged or inoperable control systems by converting them into a usable format with the help of machine learning. By integrating the weighted averages of these controllable units, the CSEW method provides a robust estimate of the treatment's aggregate impact, even within unbalanced data sets. Additional theoretical analysis confirms the CSEW method's ability to produce fair estimates, accompanied by a supporting simulation demonstrating its ability to produce just and fair estimates. Finally, the CSEW method is illustrated by re-examining the economic impact of damage to a Texas chemical plant in 2019 following a violent attack. The CSEW method found that the plant's damage resulted in a significant $3.1 billion in lost output, a finding supported by 80% of the sample. This outcome reflects the CSEW method's effectiveness in creating fair and accurate estimates even within unbalanced data. Additional case studies have verified the CSEW method's validity in creating equivalent causal estimates as balanced datasets. Consequently, we introduce the first method for protecting graph data under differential privacy, which involves encoding node data using a packetized approach, applying a cryptographic protocol to communicate randomly, and decoding at the central location to reconstruct the graph. This method involves a trade-off between protecting the graph data and preserving its density. A numerical decoding threshold is established to gauge the fidelity of graph data and social network complexity is used as a reference point for optimal graph density recovery. Accurate generalization from a limited number of training samples relies on quality.  Unfortunately, poor quality data distort this capability in real-world applications.  A novel framework we introduce improves the likelihood that the model generalizes well to unseen categories by leveraging the observation that outliers impair this capability.  Based on the idea that outliers contaminate the data distribution for a specific class, we use the prototypical loss function to train the model on the majority class samples, with the option to adjust the margin to further mitigate outlier influence.  The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated in the few-shot learning scenario on public datasets.  By mitigating outlier influence, our method yields enhanced few-shot learning performance.  The method's code is freely accessible on our GitHub profile page at https://github.com/FarhanGhammac/fsl_framework.  The approach can also be used to develop an outlier-robust baseline model for supervised learning.  Applying the method to the MNIST dataset yields the baseline model freem from contamination.  Consequently, this model exhibits improved performance over the standard CNN model on the MNIST dataset.  Ultimately, our method contributes to the advancement of reliable, real-world few-shot learning applications.  The work presented herein forms part of the Ph.D. thesis entitled 'Reliable Few-Shot Learning: A Reliable Option' which is available at https://www.adiwasi.co.in/farhan/thesis. This capability to measure classification reliability may be utilized to facilitate various astronomical data analysis procedures. Specifically, it enables identification of rare events that fall outside of a standard model's scope. To illustrate this, we present a case study involving the detection of supernovae utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks. Compared to a standard Neural Network without uncertainty quantification capabilities, we observed a substantial increase in identifying novel, previously unseen supernovae utilizing Bayesian Neural Networks. This case study demonstrates how employing Bayesian Neural Networks for astronomical supernova detection yields improved results, specifically a $28.0\%$ rise in discovering new class members and a $66.7\%$ increase in accurately verifying already known members. Bayesian Neural Networks proved compatible with current state-of-the-art supernova classifiers. The study of mechanical waves in solid crystals is significantly enhanced by the application of group theory, which helps identify and classify various mechanical modes based on their associated symmetries. Building upon this framework, this research extends the analysis to photonic crystals, focusing on the intermodal Brillouin interactions that occur due to mechanical mode coupling. By analyzing a two-wave mixing system in a crystal with specific mechanical properties, this study demonstrates that mechanical modes of distinct symmetries can lengthen or suspend specific interaction pathways. This phenomenon is exemplified through an in-depth analysis of a microresonator with a rectangular shape, whose mechanical and phononic properties are thoroughly examined. This study finds that mechanical modes of lower symmetry are more effective at slowing or suspending certain types of Brillouin interactions, particularly those involving mode swapping in a square-lattice pattern, while mechanical modes of higher symmetry are more effective at prolonging Brillouin interactions, such as those involving pentagonal and hexagonal patterns. This study presents a design for a microresonator with modified mechanical properties, stating that through mechanical optimization, it is feasible to control optical interference and polarisation dependence, making it an attractive design for various applications. Conversely, this study also identifies scenarios in which mechanical modes of lower symmetry can amplify certain types of interactions, such as Brillouin bonding modes in a square-lattice pattern, and notes that mechanical optimization can also be used to suspend or amplify these interactions. This study proposes a novel method of controlling polarization dependence through mechanical optimization, a valuable feature for optical microresonators. Furthermore, this study finds that optical interactions within the structure can be described using a combination of Bloch modes, Rayleigh-Fourier expansion, and Wannier transformation. Upon simplification, this study discovers that a particular type of optical interaction, namely Bragg-like interactions, dominates the system due to periodic variations in the refractive index. This study also finds that mechanical optimization can be used to either prolong or suspend these Bragg-like interactions. A notable finding of this study is that mechanical modes of lower symmetry can make Bragg-like interactions more pronounced near band edges, a phenomenon that may be valuable for certain applications where large fabrication tolerances are required. Conversely, this study also makes another notable finding that mechanical modes of higher symmetry can make Bragg-like interactions more susceptible to perturbations, a phenomenon that may be beneficial for reducing optical interference within the structure. This study proposes a design for a microresonator with modified mechanical properties, a valuable feature for controlling polarization dependence

The findings presented address key theoretical questions about the generalized standard elements within classical finite Coxeter groups. Specifically, we demonstrate the exchange properties of a generalized standard element for type Bn can be represented by a periodic pattern, related to its length and set of descents, and extend the properties of the involutions present in type An by introducing 'n-th difference' involutions for type Bn, with analogous properties for type Dn. Moreover, we precisely identify the elements in type Bn that can be expressed as a product of the elements from its subgroups known as parabolic type Bn minus 2, and analogous results apply to type An and Dn. Lastly, we describe the elements in type Bn that can be expressed as a product of the elements from its subgroups known as fidelties, by inverting its standard involutions, and analogous results apply to type An and Dn. In recent years, the integration of constraint programming with heuristics has become increasingly significant in solving complex practical problems. This research focuses on two hard optimization problems, the Steiner Ulybin-Kovalenko problem and the Binary Mixed Ulybin-Kovalenko problem, which were originally proposed in 2003 as purely theoretical challenges. To effectively tackle these issues, we employ a local search algorithm, E2LS, where LS is based on a constraint programming model with virtual nodes, and E2 incorporates two specific heuristics. Our analysis demonstrates that E2LS exhibits enhanced efficiency compared to other methods, such as virtual node ant colony, multi-agent search, and simple local search, in both high- and low-vertex connectivity scenarios. Additionally, E2LS is used to establish lower bounds for these problems via multi-agent path problem formulations, and it achieves near-optimal solutions for instances with up to 21 vertices, as well as exact solutions for instances with up to 16 vertices. This method also computes high-quality approximate solutions for larger problems. For instance, in the case of a 25-vertex graph, E2LS yields a solution within an optimality gap of 0.23%, and for a 31-vertex graph, the result is a solution within an optimality gap of 0.46%. Since 2003, when the SUKP and BMCP were first proposed, this research represents the current best approximate and exact algorithms for these problems. Furthermore, in the context of multi-agent path problems, our findings surpass previous works published by Janson and Rolf in 2009 and by Nair and Rolf in 2012. Interestingly, in the scenario of low-vertex connectivity, our approach differs from an ant colony optimization algorithm studied by Nair and Rolf in 2012, yielding better results, and for high-vertex connectivity, our approach surpasses a multi-agent search algorithm explored by Janson and Rolf in 2009, also resulting in better outcomes. This research also includes a detailed analysis comparing the computational efficiency of E2LS, a global optimization algorithm, with that of a multi-agent search, a local search, and ant colony optimization algorithms in the context of the SUKP for instances with 6, 7, and 8 vertices. In numerous studies and applications across various domains, the concept of predicting future behavior has been developed. Focusing on the industry of telecommunication, our objective is to create a tool for determining which customers are likely to discontinue their service by comparing their historical data patterns to that of loyal customers. To achieve this, we use time-series analysis techniques to build and evaluate different models, leveraging the concept of Kalman Filter as a framework. The underlying idea is that these models can serve as a real-time change detection system, where the dynamics of each customer can be consistently monitored and adapted based on new observations. The adaptability and shift in behavior can indicate potential disengagement signals. The practical outcomes of this research include an operating system for analyzing customer change dynamics, as well as actionable alerts for telecommunication companies to retain vital customers. The research further highlights the importance of the length of historical data used for training and testing, as longer histories often lead to better prediction accuracy and lower false positive and false negative rates. The theoretical basis of this research is rooted in the Kalman Filter model, which is usually applied in control systems for robotic arms and space probes but, in this context, focuses on analyzing the state of intangible resources such as customer satisfaction. The methodology described can be easily integrated into other communication platforms and systems to analyze and predict various resource dynamics. The practical challenges and solutions in implementing this methodology are discussed, including data sampling, feature extraction, and self-adaptation. Finally, the social implications and contributions of this research are outlined, focusing on providing valuable insights for decision-makers to retain customers and improve customer satisfaction, which is a critical issue in the telecommunication industry. The emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) can further facilitate the implementation of our research by integrating smart devices that analyze and predict various resource dynamics. The bounds of technology can be explored and optimized to analyze the dynamics of human emotions, environment, and other complex systems, leading to improved decision-making and resource management. The methodology described can be easily adapted to various applications, such as predicting failure in machines, detecting diseases, forecasting electricity consumption, estimating revenue, and many more. The theoretical concepts and measurement methods discussed can provide valuable insights to application developers and owners to preserve their valuable resources, as well as detect, prevent, and isolate resource failures. The practical outcomes and results of this research can be accessed through a web interface, located at http://dtms.utech.edu.jm. The software framework is open-source and can be freely obtained at http://dtms.ute

We are investigating the effect of the irrelevant operator $L_{-4}\bar L_{-4}\lambda$ on the integrability of the effective $\sinh^2$ theory in the context of Ising Field Theory, specifically at a level of order. When we take the ultraviolet limit, the operator transforms into a relevant one, $\cos 2\phi\lambda$. This means the high-energy behavior of the theory is determined by a set of universal relevant operators. Notably, the shift of the magnetic magnetic susceptibility, $\delta h$, is governed by a specific relevant operator, $e^{2\alpha\sigma}\phi\lambda$. When we calculate the shift up to fourth order, we verify its concordance with the series expansion of the two-loop Bethe ansatz results. This confirms the presence of a specific relevant operator within the $\sinh^2$ theory. Additionally, the presence of the irrelevant operator leads to a non-existent conformal coupling between the dual pairs of twist fields. This further reinforces the notion that the relevant operator, $\cos 2\phi\lambda$, defines the high-energy behavior of the theory. Ultimately, our analysis provides a framework for determining the relevant operator in effective theories derived from conformal field theories, specifically in the context of $\sinh^2$ theories. This framework has broader implications and can be applied to various models. This research develops a strategy for computing the gluon TMDPDFs on a lattice by relating them to the colored twist-angle eigenstates of the Wilson line operators. With the established scheme, we demonstrate the connection between the Berwein-Schaefer-Van Neerven-Collins arneit TMDPDF and a novel set of gluon TMDPDFs. We further obtain the factorization formula for the arneit TMDPDF in terms of the gluon TMDPDFs, which allows us to compute the latter on a lattice. This breakthrough enables a direct connection between the Berwein-Schaefer-Van Neerven-Collins arneit TMDPDF and a linear combination of its gluon counterparts, which aids in identifying the correct combination of gluon TMDPDFs required for factorization. This development is particularly valuable when working with arneit TMDPDF that lacks a field-theoretic counterpart for the twist-2 contribution. Ultimately, this strategy opens up a new pathway for computing gluon TMDPDFs that are not accessible via field-theoretic treatments. Additionally, it facilitates the direct comparison between the arneit TMDPDF and the conventional gluon TMDPDFs with the same twist angle, which is typically used in experimental analyses. We include appendices detailing additional background information, incorporating insights from the arneit TMDPDF's field-theoretic analysis, and providing an illustration of its application. Furthermore, our analysis in this paper highlights a novel application of Wilson line operators, which have been extensively explored in recent years, particularly those in the context of the QCD factorization theorem. Cyclist safety enhancement through data collection helps identify potential risks in city cycling infrastructures. Traditionally, data collection procedures have focused either on gathering information or ensuring safety, but not both simultaneously. This paper introduces a novel approach, combining cycle monitoring with data harvesting, to create a dataset that improves cycling safety in urban environments. This innovative cycle data platform, powered by IoT technology, includes a smart analytics component that generates actionable insights for city planners to design more secure roads for cyclists. The developed framework has been tested on a 10 km route in Hyderabad, India. The evaluation results demonstrate its effectiveness in generating valuable cycle data for urban cities in developing countries. The created dataset, comprising of 337 users and 25,281 cycles, has been made publicly available for research purposes on SharePoint. Additionally, 21 critical points of concern, affecting cycle users, have been identified based on the gathered data. Finally, we present future research opportunities based on this data. This study introduces a path planning method tailored for distributed autonomous robots that utilizes a real-time control strategy to account for model uncertainties. Key considerations in this distribution-agnostic approach include a robust control design that ensures the robot remains on track despite model uncertainty, and a direct control allocation method that avoids reliance on a pre-defined feasible trajectory. Furthermore, a specific path planning law is proposed to address the challenge of maintaining a predetermined distance from obstacles while mitigating the effects of model uncertainty and sensor data noise. Simulated scenarios in two distinct settings, coastal fishing net navigation and ring race, serve as case studies to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficacy of the proposed path planning method. Notably, these case studies highlight the potential benefits of a robust path planning approach in achieving proven stable results, even in the presence of significant model uncertainty. In the coastal fishing net scenario, this path planning method achieves an impressive result, bringing the robot within a 0.05 meter radius of the target destination over a period of time. In the ring race scenario, this path planning method achieves an impressive result, bringing the robot within a 0.1 meter radius of the target destination, despite a substantial model uncertainty of 25%. This integrated design, which combines a direct control allocation method and a specific path planning law, demonstrates robustness to model uncertainty in both two and three-dimensional space. This method also ensures a consistent and reliable performance, even when encountering uncertainty. Notably, this method only relies on the robot's sensors for real-time feedback and does not use a pre-defined feasible trajectory. As a result, this method enjoys substantial freedom from constraints. Overall, this path planning method is shown to be an efficient and reliable solution that consistently achieves desirable results. In the coastal fishing net scenario, this method successfully navigates uncertainty, completing the task at a speed of 0.5 meters per second. In the ring race scenario, this method successfully navigates uncertainty, completing the task at a speed of 1.5 meters per second. In comparison to conventional methods, this path planning method delivers superior performance, even when encountering uncertainty. Notably, this method successfully demonstrates robustness to model uncertainty, completing the coastal fishing net and ring race tasks within 27.9 and 101.8 seconds, respectively. We've developed a novel method for approximating the conditional distributions of Gaussian processes by leveraging deep learning. Our approach relies on the understanding that a Gaussian process's posterior can be optimized for sequential data by propagating errors from the prior through the data points. This leads to a pathwise conditioning effect, where the GP's uncertainty is systematically reduced as more data is collected, without relying on iterative optimization or model assumptions. Instead, we use a small set of learnable vectors and a GP prior to make predictive statements. The vectors are updated using a closed-form formula that reflects the intersection of all possible GP posteriors, offering a universal improvement over starting with the prior. This method, called full Gaussian process conditioning, outperforms conventional techniques on a range of tasks, even at the initial data collection stage. The code is freely accessible at full-gp-conditioning.github.io. Our research implies that conventional optimization methods may fail to find the full posterior's optimal subset when the prior is suboptimal. We derive this theory by analyzing the GP with a finite number of random variables and demonstrate that a similar effect occurs in finite GP implementations, where the pathwise conditioning effect is recovered when using larger datasets. The pathwise conditioning effect is preserved across various GP approximations, such as kernel ridge regression, random feature approximation, and deep Gaussian process techniques. Furthermore, it enables a unbiased, pathwise conditioning strategy for stochastic GP regression that outperforms existing methods. The methodology and empirical results are demonstrated for regression problems, but theoretically apply to classification and other GP applications. By systematically reducing the GP's uncertainty, the pathwise conditioning effect offers a more nuanced understanding of the Gaussian process and opens the door to a range of novel applications and techniques. The pathwise conditioning effect is distinguished from related concepts in GP inference, such as the Kalman filter, ensemble sampling, and probabilistic regression, in which the propagation of errors is either assumed or requires model specificity or priors. As a consequence of our approach, the pathwise conditioning effect is seen as an adaptive, universal method of GP posterior optimization that is compatible with various dimensions, model types, priors, optimization techniques, and approximation methods, and is thus universally applicable to the Gaussian process. The proposed network aims to achieve high data rate transmission while ensuring reliable connectivity, using the UAVs as mobile connectivity points. Initially, the received signal power is calculated using a modified Two-Ray model, specifically designed for the UAV ground system. Next, the error is minimized by developing a weighted least squares method for channel tracking. To compensate for the increasing noise with distance, frequency inversion is incorporated into the model. The performance of the proposed model is evaluated using simulations, which compare the results of the LMMSE-SOSTC, TOSTC, and normal least squares methods. Notably, the output of the new model exhibits better performance than its counterparts when testing for large distances. The success of the approach is further demonstrated by successful data decoding using the LMMSE-SOSTC algorithm, while the LOSTC and normal least squares methods experience increased BERs with increasing distance. Overall, the new model showcases the potential for the LMMSE-SOSTC algorithm to achieve accurate channel estimation and data transmission. The work is then validated by another set of simulations, which incorporate real-world environments, and the outcomes confirm the suitability of the approach for diverse terrestrial communication systems. The outcome has significant implications for the design of the UAV communication network, allowing it to function effectively in various scenarios, even with the UAVs moving at high speed, terminating the connection at will, and the presence of interference. The capability of the approach to function properly on platforms with distinct trajectories has also been validated, allowing the UAVs to achieve deep penetration into the network area while maintaining connectivity with ground devices. The outcome underscores the promising potential of the UAVs as reliable connectivity points to establish a connection between the aerial and ground communication systems, facilitating seamless data transmission between them. The benefits of static elimination for memory safety in imperative languages like C are extensive. A related, less studied area involves its application to functional programs, specifically those that incur dynamic binding with function references. This paper showcases a novel, strict type system designed to ensure the safe dismissal of functions in functional programs, achieving this goal with a decidable framework. The type system incorporates polymorphism and type inference, ensuring that functions can be safely terminated without posing undecidable demands on the type system or compromising functional properties. Furthermore, we integrate this approach within a fully functional programming language called Fun, which allows for advanced memory management through explicit allocations and dereferences. This language serves as a testing ground for the introduction of a novel, strict type system and other related safety features. The type system and language design are presented in conjunction with a formalization of their rules and an implementation, both of which are combined to verify their soundness through a formal proof. The paper also discusses how to efficiently eliminate certain low-level functions in the language, highlighting issues of function currying and uncurrying, and how it impacts memory safety. The type system and language design highlighted several novel challenges, including the safe termination of functions containing cyclic references in the presence of polymorphism, achieving a fully functional strict type system, and addressing function currying and uncurrying. The final result contributes a simple algorithm for eliminating functions in a high-order sublanguage of the $\lambda_{\rm{SI}}$ calculus, specifically the extended version with let-rec, by demonstrating that any well-typed Fun program with a safe reference structure can be converted into a $\lambda_{\rm{SI}}^{\rm{rec}}$ expression. The paper concludes that its proposed approach offers a promising solution for ensuring the safe termination of higher-order programs containing cyclic references, a long-standing problem in static program analysis, and proposes a new promising solution. The potential of nonlinear co-addition techniques for removing cosmic rays in HST images has been explored. Median and clipped-mean algorithms were tested alongside traditional sigma-clipping, with a key focus being the maintenance of a consistent point spread function (PSF) across all stars. However, median and clipped-mean proved ineffective in preserving the PSF profile, particularly for larger stars where the nonlinear effects become substantial. Consequently, these nonlinear methods are likely unsuitable for cosmic ray removal in astronomical images. On the other hand, sigma-clipping, particularly when combined with secondary maxima analysis, demonstrates considerable potential in effectively co-adding images free of cosmic rays, with a notable success rate of 85% for a specific test sample of F814W images. This technique, paired with secondary maxima analysis, outperforms primary maxima analysis in sigma-clipping by approximately 20% in terms of co-adding efficiency. Furthermore, we identify regions within the PSF core as the most challenging area for cosmic ray detection, with a notable success rate of only 35% in this area, which presents an interesting area for further improvement. We also observe an interesting co-addition behavior in this PSF core region, where a secondary peak emerges due to diffraction effects, potentially contributing to the development of more sophisticated cosmic ray detection and removal techniques in the future. With these findings, we conclude that sigma-clipping, accompanied by secondary maxima analysis, is a practical and efficient method for cosmic ray removal in HST images. We have also made available a Python version of this method, named CRifter, for the use of the astronomical community. Finally, we reflect on the shortcomings and difficulties associated with cosmic ray detection and the potential of combining artificial intelligence and advanced image processing techniques to address these challenges in future developments.

A blockchain consensus protocol, LC4IoT, has been designed for applications involving physical world data in supply chain management. This protocol utilizes a consensus mechanism that incorporates a unique layer, enabling the creation of a blockchain that is 'physically aware'. The protocol leverages the principles of fuzzy logic to generate abstract representations of IoT data, which are utilized within a fuzzy state transition model to generate a unique consensus layer. This layer incorporates weight calculation based on fuzzy states and a proposed design for achieving final consensus. The efficacy of LC4IoT is evaluated under various conditions of network normalcy and adversarial settings. The results demonstrate its ability to optimize final consensus time and minimize energy consumption while maintaining optimal levels of accuracy. A comparison with other consensus protocols further underscores the efficacy of LC4IoT. The protocol has the potential to integrate with existing blockchain frameworks with minimal modification, making it easily adaptable across various platforms. The integration of the protocol with a fuzzy logic layer results in a notable increase in accuracy and resource efficiency. Designing a robust automated image analysis system requires an in-depth understanding of the forms a cell may take, which is a challenge that has not been fully resolved. Current techniques used for cell shape synthesis, tracking, and detection lack efficiency, mainly because of the limited availability of accurate models to guide their development. To address this issue and create a more unified analysis framework, we present a new deep learning approach for synthesizing realistic curves representing single-celled organisms. This technology enables the creation of synthetic data to enhance the performance and reliability of cell shape detection, recognition, and tracking systems. After training our model using curves from the Cytoskelet-On database, it successfully passed a rigorous test, generating curves that were almost indistinguishable from real ones based on both visual and statistical inspections. Furthermore, by utilizing our model to create synthetic training data, we were able to significantly improve the accuracy of a system designed to detect and follow the movements of a type of single-celled organism called Volvocaria. When our method was used to create data, the volume of false data removed increased by an average of 71%, while the overall detection and tracking errors decreased by around 29% compared to the standard method. This study demonstrates the value of a system for generating synthetic data of cell shapes and highlights the potential of this technology to unify and facilitate image analysis in the biomedical field. For print-disabled users, particularly those with difficulties in reading Braille, the efficient navigation through 3D printed models of scientific documents holds great significance. Researchers in this field have made considerable progress in employing vision-based techniques. Yet, these systems still struggle to deal with complex internal references that span across multiple pages. To address this issue, this study introduces an advanced data-driven model, which combines information about page images and XML codes, to accurately identify and manage such references. The proposed solution incorporates a novel technique to sequence a vast array of reference candidates based on the reference system specified in XML and the visual connections between images on different pages. The researchers evaluated the accuracy of this approach using a dataset compiled from 40 books and achieved satisfactory results, demonstrating its effectiveness and reliability. The outcome showcases the ensemble of human-curated XML data and computer-learned image features as a powerful tool in enhancing the accuracy of vision-based techniques. Building on this success, the researchers are confident that it will significantly benefit print-disabled users by offering more reliable assistance in reading 3D printed scientific documents through vision-based technology. The associated code and data can be accessed through a publicly accessible GitHub repository. Additionally, a live demonstration of the proposed system will be presented at the workshop.

As high-precision radial velocity surveys uncover diverse planetary orbits, the need arises for spectroscopic analysis techniques that can distinguish stellar contamination from actual planetary spectra while identifying unique planetary features. We developed an advanced high-resolution spectroscopic analysis program using PyAOS, grounded in the Reynolds Operator, to achieve this goal. By leveraging the Reynolds Operator, our software optimizes spectral combinations and pinpoints distinct spectral patterns. In our analysis, the PyAOS program demonstrated its ability to accurately recreate synthetic spectra with minimal errors in spectral combinations, even in the presence of varying orders. Notably, in comparisons with the specifications of current high-resolution spectrographs, the PyAOS program yielded errors within 0.05-0.20 angstrom for its spectral combinations. Moreover, a cross-validation test involving the high-resolution spectra of hot stars from the Hamburger Rössle-Spectra database showed the PyAOS program's ability to identify and extract hot star spectra with high accuracy. Our initial study highlights the potential of the PyAOS program to dissect and break down high-resolution spectra of stars and hot objects into their underlying components. This is particularly significant for future high-resolution spectroscopic surveys, which will be pivotal in high-precision radial velocity spectroscopy, enabling the identification of planetary features and distinguishing stellar contamination. As a result, our survey will significantly contribute to the optimization of future surveys, enabling the identification of planetary features and uncovering diverse planetary orbits while refining our understanding of stellar composition. Additionally, our software can be adapted and utilized in other high-resolution spectroscopic surveys, such as those involving astrobiology, exo-biology, and other related research fields. Future research will see the application of the Reynolds Operator in analyzing high-resolution spectroscopic data obtained using the TESI at the GTC. Furthermore, our software has the potential to be utilized in the analysis of other high-resolution spectrographic data, enabling comparisons between different datasets and instrumental configurations. In our study, a fully adaptive solution is proposed, combining an adaptive mesh refinement algorithm with robust threat metrics. To validate the model's capabilities, simulations are conducted on various test cases, including a scenario modeled by Mead (1976) in the central Pacific, and comparisons are made with observed data from the 2018 Cullee Landslide Tsunami in Alaska, USA. The findings demonstrate that the proposed model achieves a satisfactory balance between depth and time resolution, leading to plausible results that align with the characteristics of the observed tsunami waves. This research offers an original and efficient solution for simulating tsunami waves, allowing for the modeling of non-trivial non-linear tsunami dynamics. It provides an effective tool for various engineering and scientific applications, such as evaluating Structure Integrity, Coastal Vulnerability Risk Analysis, and Seismological Data Inversion. Detecting very massive galaxies above 10 billion light-years away is key 
to conducting a cosmic census during the epoch of reionization. So far, the 
galaxies with the highest masses observed at redshifts greater than three have 
primarily been identified through observations of a specific wavelength of 
light, but these galaxies are often missed by infrared space telescopes 
operating at present times. Our study reveals a massive galaxy located nearly 
15 light-years away from its neighboring galaxy from a group called ACS-HS3. 
This 100 billion times more massive system has been observed using a technique 
called gravitational lensing that makes it appear much brighter to us. By 
studying it, we found the galaxy was forming stars quickly at a rate many 
times more massive stars than our own Milky Way, but less than half as much 
massive stars as a different type of system called a starburst. These data 
together with observations of how the light from the stars left the galaxy 
indicate the stars formed at a rate that should have heated the surrounding 
gas and made the light appear different when we look at it. What we actually 
see instead is the light from these stars being blocked by something, 
suggested to be dust, indicating there is a lot of dust hiding deep within 
the galaxy. This discovery supports theories saying that massive galaxies were 
formed from smaller stars eating each other up, and also that starburst 
galaxies are not the only ones quickly forming stars as previously thought. 
Our study also means these types of galaxies are not as rare as previously 
believed. Using a model to calculate how many of these types of systems 
exist, we found their total mass is about the same as their total luminosity 
at their peak. This conclusion aligns with observations suggesting these types 
of galaxies are not the only ones quickly forming stars as their light will 
soon be seen at many different wavelengths of light. Our study also means these 
types of galaxies are not as rare as previously thought and could help 
explain how, when the universe was just 900 million years old, all the 
light-producing matter became hidden from our view through a process called 
reionization.

To study the impact of rate dependence in inelastic material regions, we apply the internal variable formulation of rate-dependent damage mechanics to an elastic material, mimicking plasticity behavior. This model is unique as it does not establish a connection between internal time and external time, instead making the history of internal variables relative to the material. We investigate this model within small-scale material science, utilizing a small-deformation framework that simplifies the model to a nonaffine, rate-dependent damage accumulation, influenced by the distance between fibrils. By comparing simulations to experimental outcomes from three different experiments on an adhesive tape, we verify that the model's nonaffinity is evident in its experimental applications, particularly at low deformation rates. Furthermore, we show that the model's experimental predictions could potentially differ from those based on affine models, especially at rates below 0.1/s. This outcome presents an opportunity for microscopic experiments to validate the model's nonaffinity and encourage the design of materials responding differently to material and external times. In conclusion, we outline potential challenges in experimenting with material histories and suggest that experiments observing the movements of defects over time could be an efficient method to study rate-dependent properties of inelastic materials. Additionally, we provide a basic explanation for why biological soft-tissues often exhibit rate dependence and outlay future research to investigate rate-dependent damage in this context, specifically in how rate-dependent properties might enhance or diminish tissue stability. As such, we introduce a concept resembling statics of external ages, applicable to media where the evolution of internal variables is governed by the external variable's age, rather than time. We outline potential applications and challenges in experimenting with rate-dependent properties of soft-tissues and highlight unresolved questions, such as formulating principles for rate-dependent properties of soft-tissues, their interaction with biochemical degradation processes, and potential database development. We conclude that rate-dependent properties of soft-tissues pose an intriguing area of research that might be beneficial for treating and managing diseases such as time-dependent material fatigue. By designing materials that counter time, one could oppose the clock and reverse the material's degradation process. We propose that a deeper understanding of rate-dependent properties is essential for understanding and developing material design rules that counter external time, thereby opposing the clock and rendering both external and material times irrelevant. Furthermore, we suggest that a structure that counter external time may be used to counter material time as well, thus rendering both clocks irrelevant. By opposing external and material times, we outline the basic principles for a novel strategy in biomedical research and technology, specifically the treatment and management of diseases

We have developed the HyperExpan algorithm, a groundbreaking approach to
automatically expand taxonomy by linking entities to unsupervised, externally
derived taxonomies. Our proposed method employs graph embedding,(Http://research.microsoft.com/pubs/Microsoft/TR-MSRTR-2014-124.pdf)
followed by ranking and selection, to identify relevant relationships between the
original and target taxonomies. In a pioneering application of word2vec to
taxonomy, HyperExpan uses word2vec embeddings for entities within the original
taxonomy to facilitate linking with the target concepts. Furthermore, our
approach introduces several innovative methods, including (i) HyperExpan's
capacity for handling hypernymy relationships at various levels of hierarchy; (ii)
the algorithm's ability to select only the most relevant concepts for each
entity; and (iii) the system's capability to perform accurate mapping between
taxonomic hierarchies with differing levels of granularity. As demonstrated by
our results on an extensive dataset comprising Wikipedia's taxonomy and a set of
selected superset taxonomies available on the web, HyperExpan outperforms a
baseline algorithm by Anselmo and Stankovic in both precision and coverage. Our
outcome indicates that HyperExpan's process of taxonomy expansion is
considerably more subtle than that of Anselmo and Stankovic, as reflected in
experiments we conducted to validate their components. Notably, a single query to
Wikidata, triggered by a findSimilarTo function, is sufficient to link each
entity of the original taxonomy to concepts of the target taxonomy, making
HyperExpan's process virtually human-sensing in terms of its applicability. 
HyperExpan, a method we developed, has been successfully demonstrated in a
interactive online application where users can contribute to its training by
tagging entities with corresponding categories from a predefined set.

We assessed and compared the performance of density functional methods in predicting various electric properties (dipole moment, isotropic hyperpolarizability, and anisotropy) of molecular dimers. The results showed that a specific hybrid functional, combined with a non-local correlation correction, yielded the most accurate predictions. In contrast, traditional density functional approximations failed to match the accuracy achieved with the NLC method. The outcomes also revealed a significant discrepancy between the outcomes of periodic and single-point calculations, indicating the necessity of utilizing the same exchange-correlation kernel for both methods to ensure the integrity of the results. Furthermore, the research highlighted the necessity of conducting thorough convergence tests when employing density functional methods. Notably, the predictions obtained with the NLC method aligned well with the results from coupled-cluster theory, particularly for dimers with minimal dispersion interactions. However, substantial deviations were observed in the case of dimers with pronounced dispersion interactions, likely due to the shortcomings of present density functional methods in accounting for these interactions. Overall, the research suggested using the NLC method for estimating electric properties of molecular dimers when coupled with a comprehensive benchmark from high-level ab initio calculations. The research findings also offer valuable insights for further refinement of density functional methods. The study's results have been made publicly available through a supporting information database, allowing for a reliable assessment of density functional results for approximately 370 molecular dimers across different types of interactions and properties. The research data can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.5194/ac.xxxxxxx.2022. (Publication is in progress)

Building upon this finding, we demonstrate the existence of a uniformly bounded estimate for the solutions over a broader class of nonnegative initial conditions. Moreover, we establish that the solutions converge uniformly towards a unique, classical solution of a limiting parabolic equation as the diffusion coefficient approaches zero. This research is an extension of our prior work focused on a similar equation in one-dimensional space, and incorporates recent advances in the two-dimensional case, including new estimates for the rate of convergence. A notable aspect of this work involves deriving precise bounds on the spatial derivative of the solutions, thereby validating a conjecture raised by Jimenez and the first author regarding the nature of the resulting polynomial estimates. In numerous fields, probabilistic entropy serves as a fundamental measure of uncertainty, also applied to evaluate security levels; however, a standardized quantification of uncertainty remains absent. This work investigates two widespread methods of uncertainty quantification: the arithmetic and geometric means. The increasing availability of lidar technology has significantly accelerated the adoption of 3D point clouds in various applications. Concurrently, deep learning-based methods have gained prominence in place recognition, but they are often confined to specific platforms and are impractical for real-time execution when employing complex architectures. Moreover, real-world lidar data poses challenges to place recognition due to its noisy and sparse spatial distribution. To overcome these limitations, we propose an efficient place recognition framework that leverages the combination of Normal Distributed Transform (NDT) and deep neural networks. Initially, a point cloud is segmented and normalized using the NDT representation, which greatly enhances the efficiency of place recognition and resilience to noise by condensing the sparse 3D data into a grid-based format. Subsequently, a light-weighted NDT recognition (LNR) model is utilized to identify places, which further refines the results through a close-range matching process to demonstrate the ability of the NDT representation to facilitate reliable place recognition at both near-range and global levels. Experimental results obtained on an automotive dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed LNR model over state-of-the-art place recognition methods in terms of accuracy, speed, and robustness. Notably, the LNR model achieves an accuracy of 88.5% at an average speed of 120 frames per second when processing 3D point clouds generated from the NDT representation. Interestingly, the LNR model also attains a place recognition accuracy of 84.6% when working directly with 3D point clouds, thus further validating the effectiveness of the NDT representation in place recognition. Moreover, the LNR model demonstrates impressive robustness to various adverse environmental conditions during testing, as evidenced by its ability to maintain 85.5% accuracy in both sunny and rainy environments, as well as when processing raw lidar data without color information. Notably, the LNR model also achieves consistent performance across diverse hardware platforms, as demonstrated by successful execution on a USB SSD-based neural network with an embedded CPU from Intel Corporation. Importantly, the proposed LNR model is capable of real-time execution on mobile platforms, as exemplified by its successful deployment on an Android smartphone with an integrated vision capability. To facilitate reproducible research, the proposed LNR code has been made available on the https://github.com/AntonioArlanz/Place-recognition-code repository, thus enabling seamless access to the code by the research community. The analysis of functional brain connections has predominantly relied on a pattern recognition approach that treats inter-regional effects as a background variable. However, this raises concerns because it does not accurately account for these background effects and also excludes valuable information they provide for data analysis.

In this research, we investigate whether reliable detection of differences in brain network patterns at an individual and group level relies heavily on inter-regional effects. We have also looked into whether reliable detection of differences in brain network patterns depends on the complexity of brain networks, specifically whether it is influenced by the number of connections in each network.

We conducted a comprehensive analysis involving 81 participants, dividing them into three groups. We analyzed resting-state fMRI data and removed single region effects to study inter-regional effects, focusing on variations between groups. Our results show that the complexity of brain networks significantly affect the reliability of data analysis, both at an individual and group level. This suggests that inter-regional effects are crucial for accurate analysis, otherwise, the results are not reliable. Furthermore, our study highlights crucial roles of background effects in brain network analysis, and shows that reliable detection of individual and group differences in brain network patterns heavily rely on effective analysis of background effects. 

This research sheds light on a previously overlooked aspect of brain functional connectivity, underscoring the need for an inclusive, rather than an exclusive, approach that treats background effects as an essential component rather than a disturbance. We propose that inter-regional effects be regarded as critical inter-site effects, and that effective methods such as multivariate analysis be used for their effective analysis. 

In conclusion, our findings offer a framework that can be used in a wide array of neuroimaging studies, incorporating new knowledge about the role of background effects in brain network analysis, and how it affects accuracy in data analysis. Our research holds implications for the design of a new class of multivariate-based data analysis methods that effectively utilize inter-regional effects, rather than treating them as noise. This in turn, could lead to the development of more accurate data analysis methods, and a deeper understanding of the important role background effects play in brain network analysis. 

This research is crucial because it effectively bridges the gap between pattern recognition and path analysis, incorporating key concepts from both disciplines, and sets the stage for a unique analytical framework, and could lead to the development of a new scientific discipline, namely network medicine. This research holds significant promise for the effective utilization of big data in the diagnosis and treatment of complex diseases at an early stage.

In a general distributed communication model with N stations, we examined two basic issues - a naming problem and a counting problem. The counting problem has the added requirement that each station needs to determine the total number of stations that have produced a 1, while the naming problem's only extra requirement is for each station to generate a unique identifier if it has produced a 1. The counting problem is equivalent to a naming problem with the added constraint of replicating an initial value. We developed algorithms to solve these problems in a style where only the first station knows the total count or names the other stations, and we demonstrated that our algorithms have a specific energy complexity of O(N) in the sense of Mihail. We further proved that this is a maximum lower bound in a scenario where communication is bidirectional. We also discovered a reduction problem where a distributed algorithm for the counting can be converted into a distributed algorithm for the naming, and vice versa, with a specific energy complexity of O(N). The research shows that the energy complexity of our algorithms is optimal by proving that any algorithm in a style where only the first station has additional information has a specific lower bound. We further extended the results to a scenario called protected distributed algorithms, where the main goal is to ensure that the final output of the algorithm remains unchanged even if up to one quarter of the stations malfunction, and we obtained the lower bound of O(N) in such a scenario. Robotic motion planning involving multiple obstacles is typically solved using a reconfigurable grid, which offers real-time solutions but falls short in addressing complex spatial constraints like those found in environments with overhangs or keypoints of critical importance. In this research, we introduce a novel method to generate constraints that can be used with RRT-based planners. Our approach focuses on generating constraints as a graph, which can be used to restrict the search area and generate more accurate trajectories. We then combine this method with the Standard RRT and an improved RRT algorithm, P-RTCT, which incorporates a predictive model of constraints, and evaluate their performance in a series of tests. The results show our method, in particular, outperforms existing motion planning methods in environments with complex spatial constraints. We observe a significant improvement in the average completion time of the P-RTCT algorithm, which is nearly 3 times faster than RRT, while also achieving a substantial reduction in the number of sampling collisions. We have made our code available for further research at: https://github.com/krishanagar/ spatial constraints for motion planning. The dataset used in this research can be found at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.robot.2022.103246. We have also made a ROS2 package available for navigating a maze: https://github.com/krishanagar/maze navigation. Key Words: motion planning, spatial constraints, cluttered environments, constrained motion planning, overhead navigation.

This study investigates the design of multiuser MIMO systems that utilize distributed processing to optimize sum-rate, even in the presence of channel uncertainty. To achieve this goal, a group LASSO-based approach is taken to assign tasks in the uplink, which in turn leads to a novel algorithm for downlink signal reconstruction. Furthermore, two iterative algorithms are proposed to optimize the group LASSO problem from both a centralized and distributed perspective. Our results show that the group LASSO approach not only enhances sum-rate and interference management, but also mitigates the effects of channel uncertainty. Next, a new LASSO-based metric is introduced to optimize uplink user assignment within each group, particularly to assign users that experience the least amount of interference. This modification is proven to yield better optimal solutions and also reduces the computational complexity of the algorithm. Finally, the effectiveness of the group LASSO approach is demonstrated through numerical results, which reveal an optimal balance between sum-rate and computational complexity. It is observed that the choice of parameters allows for a trade-off between sum-rate and computational complexity. Moreover, the design of the model's parameters can reveal valuable insights into the geometric structure of the feasible uplink coding and precoding matrices, which in turn paves the way for generalizing the approach to more complex interference channels. Our study shows that the group LASSO approach offers a powerful tool for optimizing multiuser MIMO settings, which can be extended to other channel models, although a remaining challenge exists in the form of a non-convex optimization problem. To address this issue, the paper explores the geometric structure of the feasible uplink coding and precoding matrices, which reveals that the optimal solutions form specific geometric manifolds. Building upon this insight, the paper proposes a new algorithm called Geom-MAD, which uses a novel method called discriminant analysis to identify key properties of the manifold. Interestingly, the study shows that the identified properties can be used to develop a new performance metric, which in turn enables the design of a publicly accessible MATLAB code for the Geom-MAD algorithm. This code facilitates a rapid and efficient identification of the geometric structure of specific manifolds, such as multiuser MIMO and SLAM channels. To further optimize these settings, the paper proposes a new approach called MAD, which uses a convex optimization problem to identify a specific point on the SLAM manifold. Our results show that the proposed metric offers an accurate generalization of previous results to more complex scenarios and also paves the way for a future study on performance metric

A modified ElGamal cryptosystem incorporating discrete logarithms over elliptic curves in torus form has been explored. Enhancements were introduced in the form of modified public keys, encrypted messages (which no longer consist of a single element), and a decreased transmission rate. Specifically, a public key is defined as a pair $\langle G_1, r \rangle$, where $G_1$ belongs to a chosen subgroup and $r$ represents a randomly chosen element. This results in a significant reduction in key size. Furthermore, the encrypted message becomes a pair $\langle \alpha \cdot m \cdot h_1^{r_1}, \beta \cdot h_2^{r_2} \rangle$, indicating a reduced transmission rate due to shared knowledge of $G_1$. Computational experiments have validated the feasibility of this framework. Enhancements were found to offer superior performance in key size and transmission rates when compared to the original ElGamal cryptosystem on similar elliptic curve systems. These improvements were found to offer a significant edge in key size and transmission rates for curves with small security levels (around 48 bits). Specifically, the modified system was found to offer a 55.71% reduction in key size for a 48-bit secure curve when compared to the original ElGamal cryptosystem, which also resulted in a 30.52% reduction in transmission rate. This gain in key size and transmission rates is expected to increase for curves with higher security levels. Furthermore, the proposed modifications demonstrate applicability and adaptability within FFC systems, where applicable. These enhancements are feasible due to a demonstrated algorithm that efficiently samples from a subset of elliptic curve points with non-torsion order $k$. This algorithm is found to work on curves with security levels ranging from 80 to 1219 bits. An alternative version of this framework was found to operate under the hard BDL problem, where both the sender and receiver possess identical public keys. This variant was discovered to offer similar performance improvements in key size and transmission rates. This version of the modified ElGamal cryptosystem was found to offer a secure and efficient solution under the considered DL problem. These developments are expected to offer a competitive alternative to original ElGamal cryptosystem, specifically in key size and transmission rates. Language models commonly address rare words by replacing them with universal words like "[UNK]" or "[ROOT]" without considering their context. This paper suggests that these words, when they do appear, have specific meanings related to the surrounding text, such as branching from a parent node in a parsing representation. We propose an approach that captures the meaning of rare words as control flow states dependent on preceding words in the sequence. This is achieved by introducing a modular aspect to word embeddings, separating them into modules corresponding to syntactic categories and control flow states. Our mechanism uses a universal aggregator to combine embeddings of rare words and their dependencies, effectively embedding the word as a control flow state conditioned on its surrounding context. Our method demonstrates that rare words can be encoded in a rare sense by relying on the encoded branch information, particularly in branch points of a parsing representation. The word embeddings in our system are adaptable to learn branch information for words, unlike traditional methods. Our model has been proven effective in controlled experiments, and also improves word representations generally when compared to state-of-the-art baselines on the task of SemEval-2018 Task 11. Additionally, our code and model are openly available for review at https://github.com/timwang12/CCFLnLM. We also release the first Chinese LMT model, trained from scratch using the new code, at https://github.com/chongxh/tf2fastText.
