Deep learning's predictive capabilities can be enhanced by assuming the distributions of its weights and biases. By assuming the distributions of its weights and biases, Deep learning's predictive capabilities can be enhanced in two significant ways. Firstly, it enables the calculation of the uncertainty of its predictions at inference time. This is particularly valuable since the reliability of predictions often correlates with their accuracy. This paper examines and compares the performance of Bayesian neural networks, Gaussian processes, and approximations like variational mode decomposition and weight sharing, using image classification experiments involving random data to demonstrate their effects. Our results show that Bayesian neural networks outperform the others. Meanwhile, we observed that variational mode decomposition can significantly reduce dimensionality while maintaining accuracy, while weight sharing significantly fails to achieve similar results. Our understanding of solar and stellar magnetic activity benefits from models based on the mean-field dynamo framework, which helps identify the critical physical parameters involved. These models, which consider the most influential turbulent effects, significantly lack precision, however, and overestimate the weight of other factors. The rapid advancements in computational power make it possible to include all turbulent effects in dynamo simulations, but this requires adapting the theoretical framework of the mean-field dynamo model to these three-dimensional simulations. Our goal is to fill this gap by developing a theoretical framework that bridges the gap between the mean-field dynamo model and three-dimensional simulations. This new framework compacts the complexity of the three-dimensional simulations into a single differential equation for the angular momentum balance. It also reveals the origin of the α-effect and explores the role of helicity input by convection. Our model shows good agreement with simulations of the α-effect and also sheds light on the mechanisms involved in dynamo processes within the Earth's core and the Sun. Our team is now planning to extend this model to include other factors such as magnetic feedback, variations in solar eccentricity and the structure of the Sun's angular momentum. Our model will also be applied to study the process of star formation and to understand how solar-like stars change over their life cycle.

Developing compact and efficient neural networks requires striking a balance between minimizing weights and optimizing network performance. Promising approaches for achieving this include using perturbation-based search algorithms, which explore the network architecture space and evaluate the results empirically. Nevertheless, such methods typically rely on costly parameter tuning to identify the optimal perturbation parameters. In this study, we propose Spartan, a novel online search algorithm that autonomously adjusts its parameters to maximize the return on investment. Spartan aims to optimize the filling process of switched-dropout networks using a straightforward, model-free method that simulates the effects of perturbation parameters on sparse networks. As a result, Spartan can train sparse neural networks in real-time on large-scale datasets, automatically selecting the most efficient settings for a given dataset and task. Our experiments with Spartan on Visual Recognition tasks demonstrate its superiority over traditional methods, including complementary approaches for optimizing sparse neural networks with Spartan as a starting point. Our sources are available on the Spartan repository at https://github.com/alexmiletic/sparten. Additionally, Spartan is now available as an open-source implementation of the evaluated methods. Our goal is to establish a community around this project to further develop Spartan by inviting contributions from the scientific audience. In the future, we aim to expand the applicability of Spartan to a broader range of tasks, such as language-based tasks, and explore the use of self-supervised learning for sparse neural networks. Although past studies have examined the severity of test smells, how developers perceive these issues and their consequences is still unclear. To address this knowledge gap, our study investigates the severity of test smells and their consequences from the perspective of developers who report finding Selenium test automation defects in their project. An online survey with 24 developers who have extensive experience with Selenium revealed their perspectives on the severity of test smells and potential consequences, including their perceived effects on program correctness and code maintainability. Interestingly, developers differ in their opinions about the severity of test smells and consequences they cause. Furthermore, actual experience with defect repair seems to influence developers' perspectives, as indicated by their responses to a post-survey questionnaire. Notably, developers who have experience repairing defects caused by test smells consider these smells to be less severe than those who don't and also more likely to impact program correctness and code maintainability. Interestingly, actual experience without defect repair tends to decrease the perceived severity of test smells and their consequences, as indicated by the developers' responses to a set of questions. A central aspect of the UK's COVID-19 Test and Trace strategy was the Test and Trace locality, which was a component of the National Health Service's public health structure. Each local tracing partnership was tasked with identifying any individuals who came into contact with someone who had COVID-19 within their area, including their workplaces, communities, and social environments. A study examining the effectiveness of these local tracing partnerships from an economic standpoint reveals that they largely failed to accomplish this goal. Utilizing a combination of contact tracing reports and testing data, the study's authors found that only 24 out of 67 local areas in England were able to achieve a self-isolation rate of 65% or higher, which was the target set by the government. Furthermore, the study reveals that the most vulnerable populations, as categorised by the Index of Multiple Deprivation, suffered from reduced testing rates and inadequate contact tracing. A primary explanation for these issues was the inadequacy of local tracing partnerships in adapting to the dynamic nature of the pandemic. In an effort to enhance the Test and Trace programme's efficiency, the study recommends the implementation of a more adaptive framework that incorporates lessons learned from the initial response to the pandemic and integrates the insights gained from the Test and Trace programme with the understanding and expertise of the National Health Service's public health structure. Specifically, we focus on the time-dependent dynamics of the excursion levels, which are the fraction of sites in excess of a given level among all random field realizations. This dynamics exhibits a first-order phase transition, where the excursion levels freeze at the level corresponding to the spherical critical radius and subsequently remain stagnant. Meanwhile, spherical percolation threshold areas also display a first-order phase transition, which correspond to the discrete values of the spherical critical radius. Moreover, both transitions share a common critical radius. The behavior of the excursion levels can be characterized by a joint distribution of the disorder and the excursion level, enabling the computation of joint distribution functions and transition probabilities. This approach allows for accurate numerical determination of the joint distribution and transition probabilities. A statistical analysis of the joint distribution for the excursion levels above the critical radius reveals a shift towards a Gaussian distribution with a mean centered on the spherical critical radius. The standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution, which represents the width of the transition, scales as a function of the number of lattice sites. Interestingly, the Gaussian distribution for standard percolation excursion levels above the critical radius, which was previously observed and analytically derived, is now confirmed and extended for spherical phase transitions. A first-order phase transition was also analytically derived for the time-dependent dynamics of the excursion levels across the spherical critical radius. This result complements the numerical derivation of a first-order phase transition within the time-independent framework for spherical percolation threshold areas. While constraints in real-world scenarios can't be disregarded, learning under constraints proves challenging, especially when specifications are unclear or there's limited data available. A promising approach involves utilizing constraints that abide by a predefined set of rules, learned through self-modifying neural networks that adhere to those rules. This research showcases how the constraints learned by such agents can be leveraged to improve performance in various scenarios. We implement a mechanism allowing other agents to discover the constraints imposed by those learned to better tackle their tasks. We test this method in a simulated environment of interconnected cities, aiming to solve a complex problem of optimal resource allocation across multiple related tasks. Our findings suggest that agents sensitive to constraints learned from peers who abided by those constraints can achieve better outcomes after interaction, whereas those using a traditional constraint-based approach might not. These results suggest that the constraints internalized by constraint-abiding agents contain valuable information useful for enhancing others' performance, even without requiring access to their decision-making mechanisms. To effectively utilize physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for making predictions in uncertain situations, it is crucial to have a measurable way to determine the reliability of their predictions. This paper proposes an improved method of estimating errors from the data itself, that enables and certifies predictions made by PINNs. By incorporating this error estimation method, which incorporates uncertainty analysis, we can incorporate additional terms into the PINNs' training objectives. This enables the model to accurately represent its own uncertainties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to both an equation with a known solution and a complex acoustics equation that models the propagation of sound waves in a pipe, where we also account for uncertain boundary conditions. The results show that this approach leads to more precise predictions and a better understanding of the uncertainty associated with these predictions. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach leads to improved large-scale simulations by reducing the need for numerous data points. Furthermore, we also utilize this approach in the prediction of long-term pipe material degradation, where Pinns are able to accurately account for uncertainty in their predictions. From a computational standpoint, we found that this approach leads to improved convergence rates. As such, this approach has the potential to be utilized in machine learning solutions that handle complex physical systems. These solutions can then make predictions with measurable levels of uncertainty, which in turn can lead to better overall decision making. Lastly, the open source code related to this approach has been made available online. This code enables researchers to use PINNs for both uncertainty analysis and error estimation. Additionally, researchers can easily incorporate uncertainty analysis into other techniques such as deep Gaussian processes, and it is hoped that this will lead to improved numerical solutions. Furthermore, the use of PINNs for determining uncertainty levels can lead to improved numerical solutions in the future. The zero-energy peak in the electronic conductance of a topological insulator, resulting from non-Majorana effects, undergoes a transformation with changing temperature. A numerical calculation based on the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation shows that this zero-energy peak shifts to a peak with finite energy at room temperature, retaining its symmetry. This study utilizes Reinforcement Learning techniques to train neural networks in the face of adversarial attacks, a problem that is also being explored by Gradient-based methods. However, the RL approach diverges from traditional gradient optimization in its framework and outcomes, and we establish a direct connection between the two by examining the role of the environment. We show that the reward function plays a key role in optimizing for resilience rather than pure accuracy. Through this lens, we gain insight into the efficacy of defensive techniques such as gradient noise and adversarial training, and we evaluate the robustness of several neural network architectures in the context of black-box and white-box attacks. Ultimately, we find that while RL and Gradient-based methods share some similarities in their outcomes, they yield robustness metrics that are uniquely characterized. These unique characteristics prompt important questions about the types of threats they are designed to mitigate, and we outline potential future directions for RL in adversarial training. This work has been accepted for publication at IJCAI 2021.

A novel alignment method between two ontologies is also refined to identify discrepancies, and confirmed concepts, roles, and hierarchies are highlighted in ontologies and the alignments, respectively. Molecular movement is a primary factor influencing thermal diffusion in systems subject to temperature fluctuations. Recent research suggests that pre-trained models such as BERT can achieve
excellent results in various tasks by fine-tuning their underlying layers.
However, the rapid growth in model capabilities correlates with increasing
computational costs, making them increasingly difficult to deploy in practice.
This study investigates whether the extensive complexity of BERT is actually
necessary in the task of automatic essay scoring by examining the relative
performance of pre-trained models and their fine-tuned variants with smaller
model sizes. We discovered that fine-tuning lighter BERT models can rival the
accuracy of the full BERT model while reducing the model by half, resulting
in a 90% decrease in inference time. Moreover, fine-tuning these lighter models
over longer training periods leads to stable convergence, ultimately surpassing
the BERT model's accuracy. We analyzed these findings using visualization tools
like Lyra and visualized word importance within the data set to gain deeper
insights into the models' decision-making processes. This research suggests that
lightweight variants of pre-trained models can serve as a superior solution for
practical applications, even if they feature fewer parameters than the BERT
model. Consequently, fine-tuning these lighter models for longer training
periods may yield improved model performance, ultimately resulting in better
outcome. Moreover, incorporating the word importance values derived from the
Light BERT model over the BERT model is anticipated to enhance the accuracy of
the essay scoring task, resulting in a 0.12, 0.11, and 0.10 F1-score boost on
three distinct test sets. The research code is openly accessible on the GitHub
platform at the following link: https.//github.com/keglasper/Light-BERT4ES. 
Furthermore, the project has obtained approval from the relevant institutional
review boards to ensure the ethical, secure, and lawful processing of the
data. We have utilized a diverse collection of data, referred to as Pooling
Resources, which comprises a composite of multiple data sets including WASC, 
SAE-G, ESNLP, and others, to streamline data preparation and facilitate the
uninterrupted execution of our research. We have also developed detailed guidelines
for the data gathering and labeling process to guarantee the privacy of the test
subjects and their guardians. 
Lastly, the final model has been made publicly available at the following
DBLP link: https.//doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-10202-8.

A straightforward strategy to address the issue of unsupervised false positive suppression involves first reducing the dimensionality of the data through feature transformation, then re-training a ranking model on a set of known data to ensure positive samples remain in the top results for a given input. However, this approach falls short for more complex machine learning models as they often exhibit high levels of variability. A better method involves leveraging the properties of dense storage to simplify a more accurate distance metric, but this too has its limitations. In this research, a new framework called DenseReRank has been developed that transforms the core machine learning task into a more effective and stable box re-ranking problem, allowing for better management of model outcomes and control over the final list of results. Moreover, this approach also facilitates the easy integration of diverse and robust ranking models into the core dense reconstruction system. To validate this concept, a range of experiments were performed including validation, cross-domain verification, cross-database evaluation, and cross-view testing, showcasing the effectiveness and robustness of this approach. A public demonstration of this framework can be accessed at https://github.com/yangming90/unsupervised-rank/., Additionally, the source code of this framework can be found at https://github.com/densereactivestack/dense-re-rank. Furthermore, the data sets utilized in the research can be found at https://github.com/densereactivestack/dense-re-rank/tree/master/data. A pre-registered summary of this research can be accessed at https://osf.io/nyvej. A previous version of this research was presented at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition in 2019, with the abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.074990. A more recent pre-print of this research can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.01947, with the associated code, data and executive summary available at https://github.com/densereactivestack/dense-re-rank. A 2019.06 updated version of this research can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.02295, with the recent 2020.04 update available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09322. A updated version of this research is currently under review at the Journal of Machine Learning Research, with the associated manuscript number 1444, with the updated version available at https://e-prints.siermuite.in/u/d8c6d

Recent advancements in deep learning have revolutionized the restoration of poor-quality music recordings. These advancements hinge on two key factors: the structure of the recurrent neural network used to process audio signals, and the quality of the training dataset. The challenge of selecting an optimal neural network structure is compounded by the need to balance the trade-off between model complexity and performance, particularly when dealing with data-related issues. Rather than relying solely on trial and error or comprehensive grid searches, a novel approach is proposed to determine the most effective neural network structure for a given dataset. This approach leverages a gradient-based method to identify the optimal model parameters efficiently. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and its ability to utilize a large music dataset to determine suitable neural network structures for a specific task. The proposed method can serve as a starting point or alternative to common techniques, particularly when dealing with data-related issues. The research aims to explore the application of deep learning in the restoration of poor-quality music recordings, a technique that has been gaining significant attention in the field of audio processing. The methodology employed in this research can be adapted for the analysis of wave signals in various fields of engineering. Furthermore, the development of a neural network structure tailored to a specific task has the potential to be applied to other real-world signal processing challenges. The source code and data used in this research are available for public review. Mounting evidence suggests that memorization plays a significant role in Neural Machine Translation (NMT), with recent research indicating attention models can improve translator efficiency by reducing dependence on excessive context. This work proposes a novel syntax-aware attention model for NMT, incorporating a syntax module to guide attention distribution based on sentence structures. By enhancing attention quality, this approach claims to improve translation fluency and orthogonality. Experiments conducted on the WMT14 English-to-German dataset demonstrate the superiority of this proposed model over baseline systems, with significant gains in translation quality for both high- and low-resource settings. Analysis of the results indicates the syntax-aware attention model exhibits improved fluency and orthogonality, with benefits sustained across various beam sizes during beam search. Interestingly, our research reveals the syntax-aware model tends to produce shorter final translations than the baseline, highlighting a further opportunity for optimization. Additionally, this work explores the effectiveness of the syntax-aware model in zero-resource settings, finding a noticeable but limited improvement in translation quality. One potential explanation for this limited gain is the current implementation's constraints: the syntax module is trained using gold-standard parse data, not parallel tree data, which may inadequately represent the complexities of the source language due to suboptimal tree alignment. Furthermore, the syntax module is currently unidirectional, meaning it can only attend to specific parts of the target sentence. Combining parallel tree data with a more sophisticated and unbiased method for training the syntax-aware model is expected to yield better translations, an area the research aims to investigate in the future. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of combining syntax and attention to improve NMT systems, with promising implications for translation quality in both high- and low-resource settings. Code to reproduce these results can be found at the link: https://github.com/zhuyixu/syntax_attention_nmt. As an additional contribution, this work introduces novel metrics for evaluating translation orthogonality and fluency. While previous research has suggested using Chao Jorzan's metric for orthogonality, this new metric claims greater precision and ease of computation. Similarly, existing methods of fluency evaluation either rely on human judgment or slow heuristics, whereas the proposed metric computes fluency with greater accuracy and without requiring manual input. On the datasets English-to-German and English-to-Chinese, the new metric yields results nearly identical to JORZAN, whereas additional experimentation on Chinese-to-English translation with the new metric reveals reduced variability between runs compared to the heuristics-based approach

Planets in certain contexts are thought to form in areas with ice accumulation within the transition zone between the inner and outer regions of a developing planetary system. The boundary where ice turns into gas and condenses into ice grains is referred to as the snow line and is an area where this process occurs. The snow line's location has significant implications for planets that form in this type of process and can also influence the types of molecules that emit light and are found in carbon-rich and oxygen-rich star systems. Recent studies have analyzed the snow lines in various types of star systems using different approaches, but a thorough examination of how varying the energy used in the calculations affects the snow lines has yet to be conducted. The energy is important in the calculations as it can affect how the gas and ice grains in the system behave, particularly in the context of planets that form in this type of process. The purpose of this paper is to examine the effects of varying energy on the snow lines in carbon-rich and oxygen-rich star systems using different types of binary system simulations and initial conditions. The findings indicate that varying energy in the system results in varying values for the time it takes for carbon monoxide to condense in the system, but a consistent value for when this process occurs in terms of stellar mass; this is in contrast to other types of binary star systems. The study further analyzes and compares the snow lines in carbon-rich and oxygen-rich star systems using different types of binary star model simulations and initial conditions to examine and compare their behavior in terms of carbon and oxygen chemistry, and the findings suggest that varying energy in the system results in distinct values for the time it takes for carbon and oxygen to condense in the system, and the boundary where this process occurs in terms of stellar mass; this is in contrast to other types of binary star model simulations and initial conditions. The study includes and discusses the implications for planets that form in this type of process in terms of carbon and oxygen chemistry, and the findings suggest that planets with liquid water in terms of carbon and oxygen could potentially form in this type of process in certain types of binary star model simulations and initial conditions; this is in contrast to other types of binary star model simulations and initial conditions. A widely accepted approach for quantum state learning involves learning basis states and reconstructing a quantum state from the measured outcomes of an optimized sequence of single-qubit measurements. Although this strategy has been successful in small systems, it is confined to estimating the state's density matrix and expectation values of specific observables. We propose an enhanced method that allows us to tailor the sequence of measurements and optimizes the estimation of a predetermined set of target observables and density matrix elements. Its performance was demonstrated on various scenarios involving single qubits and two-qubit systems, particularly focusing on measuring the entanglement between two qubits. By modifying the measurement sequence of a known protocol, we were able to enhance the precision of learning entanglement between two qubits in a Bell-diagonal state. Furthermore, we were able to optimize a sequence of measurements for a general two-qubit free fermion system to achieve the highest precision in estimating the state's density matrix and expectation values of specific observables. These results show that, with knowledge of prior information, our method offers more efficient quantum state learning compared to traditional approaches. We established an information-theoretic lower bound on the error by which our method may fall in specific scenarios. We established that our method for two-qubit systems is nearly optimal in terms of error bound, specifically within 0.15 in the relative error metric. We have developed a BERT-based framework for fair learning, which involves introducing two novel operations: transmutation and mixture mutations, in conjunction with a novel loss function called the Fair Loss. In the transmutation operation, we directly change the class labels of individuals from one group, while the mixture mutation approach randomly changes labels between different groups. Both operations aim to reduce the discrepancy in treatment outcomes between groups. However, the transmutation operation directly changes labels, whereas the mixture mutation operation randomly alters labels, thus creating more uncertainty. The Fair Loss function incorporates the predictive accuracy for the transformed labels, thus preventing data from the untransformed group from being over-fit. The framework also utilizes an adversarial approach to prevent the model from discerning group identities. Our framework's key strength lies in the fact that it balances predictive accuracy for both the transformed and untransformed groups, thus enhancing the model's ability to make accurate predictions for all groups. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our framework and its ability to outperform existing methods, particularly on sensitive attributes such as race and gender. The framework and demonstration code are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/rgwb-columbia/fairtransmutation. Evaluations were conducted using data from the UDA dataset and fair learning datasets namely, CompASs, GermanTL, and BankMarketing. Furthermore, model performance was evaluated against metrics including Accuracy, Fairness, RP, EOC, Adversarial Robustness, and Maslow's Fairness. In the context of multi-task linear regression, where a shared linear response is shared across different tasks, has been investigated. The focus is on developing algorithms that use input data efficiently, as well as analyzing these algorithms' performance. Despite the advantage of having a simple strong hypothesis, $f_0(x) = \langle \Theta_0, x \rangle$, retrieving this hypothesis from given data proves to be challenging due to its high dimensionality and task diversity. As a result, existing bounds that only consider task diversity suffer from poor guarantees in dimensionality-rich settings. Conversely, bounds that consider the entire input space incur significant performance losses when the number of tasks increases. A critical finding reveals that, to overcome these issues, the key is to control the potential loss expansion in the latent space through an appropriate choice of potential function for task diversity. An optimal potential is identified, which, when combined with a variant of Boyd's potential, results in novel and natural algorithms exhibiting improved guarantees. The novel algorithms demonstrate sample efficiency in multi-task linear regression, achieving an optimal rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\mathrm{M}_{\psi}^2 D \log N}{n}\right)$. Furthermore, the developed techniques hold promise of being adaptable to other learning problems, such as multi-task Gaussian processes, where diverse task hypotheses may play a crucial role. Concretely, a novel algorithm for multi-task Gaussian regression is presented and proven to have guaranteed performance, along with an analysis of its implications for its associated empirical risk. An implementation of the proposed algorithm for multi-task Gaussian regression is also described, along with the presentation of an accompanying study that validates its performance against established baselines on a collection of common datasets. An example illustrating the algorithm's potential further highlights its versatility in a real-world context. A later section discusses potential research opportunities related to distributed learning, where the development of algorithms that are efficient in terms of communication may be crucial, especially in settings where the availability of data is limited. An illustrative example derived from a study of Facebook's MLM platform is also presented, which further highlights existing challenges in distributed multi-task learning. A conclusion to the work follows, offering additional insights into current limitations in multi-task linear regression, attempting to pinpoint whether dimensionality or diversity is the primary obstacle, and discussing the potential for the proposed algorithm to overcome both, achieving an optimal generalization across diverse tasks of different dimensions. Research into reducing the computational costs associated with neural machine translation is thriving, and various techniques have been developed to speed up and shrink models. When applying these methods to under-resourced languages, it is unclear whether they yield similar performance improvements, and whether the outcomes depend on having large, high-quality parallel data. We investigated several compression techniques for two small languages (Sinhalese and Malay), using datasets that differ significantly in size. Our results show that certain compression methods, such as post-training quantization and Knowledge Distillation, perform more consistently than others on low-resource languages, and tend to achieve better results than those based on parallel data. A further analysis revealed that the performance gains from using these compression techniques are linked to reduced computational costs, and improve significantly as the dataset size decreases to as low as 250 parallel sentences. Overall, our research suggests that using compression techniques is a viable strategy for improving machine translation performance on low-resource languages, and for achieving better results in scenarios with limited data. We also compared the costs associated with using compression techniques on a high-resource language (German) and a low-resource language (Malay), finding that Knowledge Distillation comes close to achieving the performance achieved by training on a much larger dataset, whereas other compression methods nearly matches it. Conversely, post-training quantization and Weight permuting networks yield better results than training on a much smaller dataset, although to a slightly lower extent. Our research As a supplementary outcome, our results show that German, a high-resource language, performs similarly to Malay, a low-resource language, when evaluated using BLEU scores, highlighting an interesting anomaly. We investigated this phenomenon and found that the significant gap in performance between German and Malay, and the significant gap in word alignment between these languages, are not related to their respective statuses as high-resource or low-resource languages, and that WER and BLEU scores tell a different story about language performance. We also found that robustness metrics, such as position bias, are not linked to WER or BLEU scores, suggesting an need for reporting position bias as a translation performance metric. Our research includes the translated texts of this report from three languages into English, Sinhalese, and Malay. These translations are available online at: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O4zK_M2p1dA1TQ3CAG3o6E5bK1lL/ view. A previous model engineered using ImageNet-based pre-training techniques achieved high performance in identifying pneumonia in a specific dataset, delivering results comparable to more complex models with larger training datasets. This study demonstrates the potential to reduce the need for labeled data by approximately 50% through the implementation of specific image manipulations and optimizations. Furthermore, combining these model transformations with augmentations designed to mimic the effects of medical imaging technologies significantly decreases the necessity of labeled data, enabling the model to effectively diagnose pneumonia using imaging techniques that replicate real-world procedures. The achieved performance level in this simulated scenario is competitive with that of more advanced models, necessitating further validation to confirm its practical applications. The research also highlights potential risks in incorporating algorithms capable of creating synthetic data, as well as the issue of transferability of such techniques. Ultimately, this work contributes to the understanding and discussion of issues surrounding the creation of synthetic pneumonia images. The research code can be accessed at https://github.com/tmwm/dpi-pseudo-data. The study's findings have been accepted for presentation at the IPC 2022 conference. prompt learning. By embedding the prompt learning framework within the image
captioning framework, the results show that there are several advantages. First,
it increases the flexibility of models to adapt to a broader range of tasks,

reduces the reliance on expensive, manually-written prompts, replacing them
with prompts derived from image data, which are adjusted during fine-tuning.

prompt learning adaptation stage within the image captioning pre-training
stage. Lastly, by pre-training the model, it amplifies its ability to handle
out-of-vocabulary words, resulting in significant improvements in performance on
the COCO Captions dataset. Our full code and dataset are available on GitHub.

Causal reasoning in artificial intelligence focuses on determining cause-effect relationships, while abstract reasoning explores the underlying principles of causation (as opposed to their mechanical implementations). Our research bridges the gap between concrete causal models and the abstract concept of causation, developed by philosopher Helen Long. We introduced contrastive causation, a representation of causation that emphasizes differences, to existing AI models and found that the equilibrium notion in causal models captures key properties of contrastive causation. This led us to formulate a definition of harm that aligns with utility and outcome outcomes, demonstrating both underestimation and overestimation biases can occur in evaluating harm. Furthermore, we established that equilibrium causal models may fail to accurately measure harm in certain cases, which is why we propose incorporating contrastive causation into existing models. We have also provided initial applications of the concept of harm within decision-making, while acknowledging that the proposed theory is preliminary and requires further refinement. Our work is available at https://github.com/da-be/contrastive-causation. Valuable discussions with Prof. Michael Beitz, Prof. Michael P. Wellman, and Dr. Hadi Amiri were instrumental in its completion. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to define causation learning as the process of arriving at a morally coherent, explicit, and automatic representation of causation, integrating the expertise of AI and the underlying principles of causation. We aim to make causal reasoning machines that are morally intelligent, incorporating the advances in abstract causal reasoning. Our long-term vision is to utilize these principles in AI decision-making, similar to existing AI systems that integrate utilitarianism. Our work is part of a larger research initiative that focuses on building AI systems that incorporate the underlying principles of causation. The integration of machine learning and deep learning techniques has accelerated the analysis of large, rich datasets in a variety of field studies, ultimately driving informed conservation decisions.  This document synthesizes deep learning's applications and advancements in the field of wildlife conservation, with a focus on the use of camera trap images, acoustic sensors, and radio tracking technology. It also examines the current state of deep learning in real-time data analysis, automated monitoring systems, predator-prey dynamics prediction, species distribution modeling, and the development of virtual populations. Our review highlights the significant potential of deep learning to transform wildlife and landscape monitoring, and highlights key research pathways for further exploration. This document aims to inspire future research in the field, promoting the use of deep learning in conservation, and provides a foundation for the development of more effective monitoring and prediction tools. These tools can help reduce the current decline in wildlife populations seen around the world. To this end, the document includes recommendations for future research and highlights essential data structures and algorithms. We hope that our review provides crucial information at the intersection of machine learning and conservation biology, and serves as a reference for researchers looking to make a meaningful impact in the field. This work is part of the report from the Deep Learning for Wildlife Conservation workshop, held in association with the conference. Although speech translation models are widely distributed online, facilitating zero-shot and few-shot learning, their current techniques are limited by difficulties such as inadequate data quality, leading to reduced performance even with data augmentation. To overcome this, we have developed an approach that seamlessly integrates speech, text, and image knowledge for zero-shot and few-shot learning, drawing upon vast amounts of publicly available datasets. Initially, we pre-train a speech and language model, then cross-domain learning is implemented using the Knowledge Crossing Transformer (KCT) method, which combines speech, text, and image knowledge to produce speech translations. For zero-shot and few-shot settings, our model exhibits notable improvements, with the WMT En-De evaluation dataset showing a 9.13 WMD increase in BLEU score, and the BigBio MedMush datasets showing a significant decrease of 2.13 WMD in BLEU score when comparing our few-shot method to T0,, a leading text-to-text language model. Moreover, our model's ability to cross domain yields 9. and 7. metacritic scores in zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively, indicating a substantial improvement over other cross-domain benchmarks such as m2. Our model's speech, text, and image knowledge also enables it to successfully handle novel speech inputs with unique characteristics, in a fully zero-shot or few-shot capacity. As a result, our model's overall performance in a zero-shot and few-shot settings equals that of models trained with data specifically for the specific input speech style, i.e. data augmentation. In total, our model makes cross-domain predictions on the BigBio MedMush, a leading multilingual medical speech, text, and image datasets, and speech, text, and image knowledge from vast amounts of publicly available datasets, an outstanding achievement. We provide an overview of the rationale behind the regular heat conduction equation and its alternative variants that incorporate the concept of fading memory. These alternative equations are known as the integrated heat conduction equation, one with power rule kernel and one with exponential rule kernel. We present a direct approach to derive the power rule kernel equation by combining the static stretching rule with the standard heat equation's framework. Similarly, applying the static exponential rule leads to the exponential kernel equation. We then formulate constitutive relations for memory-dependent heat flux, first through the static stretching rule and second by inverting the time derivative of the exponential rule, and show how these relations relate to the integrated heat kernel equations. Although these equations have precise solutions only for special cases, we apply the D'Alembertian invertor to regularize them and demonstrate this regularization's effect using the "double kick" example. Furthermore, we derive a constitutive relation for the regularized case that corresponds to the "Cole-Cole" equation and an inequality that characterizes nonlinearity in the regularized context. Our method for obtaining solutions in the special cases and for generalizing the "Cole-Cole" equation extends to other integrated kernel equations with general integrands. We also compare the regularized equations with the "double kick" model based on the fractional-order variational derivative. Our discussion includes an examination of the question of whether these alternative equations truly represent heat conduction principles that deviate significantly from classical conduction principles. We offer the regularized integrated kernel equation with the power rule kernel as a potential candidate for a universal heat conduction equation, one that unifies the standard heat equation and the fourth-order fractional diffusion equation. We propose the fractional-order variational derivative framework as a general method for modeling processes that involve memory effects, including diffusion, heat conduction, and electromagnetic waves, where the integration path can be defined either in space or in time. With this unified framework, we show that well-known equations derived from alternative interpretations (e.g. "diffusive regularization," the extended Caldeira-Leggett model, the fractional extended Kaluza-Klein model) correspond to the regularized equations obtained using the variational derivative. Our method enables the derivation of general constitutive relations for memory-dependent flux for the general case and facilitates the comparison of models based on variational derivatives with those based on fractional orders. As examples of such comparisons, we derive the general constitutive relation for the regularized "Cole-Coin" equation and the "double kick" model based on the variational derivative

This research introduces an innovative method for predicting energy demand by merging "Peak" forecasts generated by Expert Panel Method with conventional "Base" forecasts derived from time-series analysis. As an enhancement to conventional forecasting, the proposed approach specifically targets areas where future renewable energy integration is highest, yet forecasting tools are still limited. We applied this protocol to the hour-to-hour load forecasting for the Australian Energy Market, a challenging task due to the data's high variability and the absence of historical matching days. Contrary to expectations, the combined forecasting approach significantly reduced error rates for medium and high load levels, but performed poorly for low loads. Notably, peak forecasting outperformed base forecasting for the highest hour of the study, highlighting the potential of using these methods for disaster preparedness and emergency planning. Following optimization protocols, the performance gap between fused and separate forecasts narrowed, suggesting the possibility of achieving similar prediction accuracy with approximately 30% fewer data. This finding is thought to be due to peak forecasting's incorporation of expert opinion and temporal pattern insights from exceptional events. The results of this study hold implications for future research and highlight the challenges associated with incorporating expert knowledge into predictive modeling systems. Lung cancer has become a major public concern due to its increasing incidence and recurrence. However, conventional lung cancer treatment methods are often inadequate. As an alternative, researchers have explored deep learning algorithms to improve treatment outcomes. In this context, we present a 3D multi-scale fully convolutional neural network model to analyze vertebral fractures from CT scans. To achieve this, we first compiled a comprehensive dataset of 305 fractures and 305 non-fracture cases from 305 patients. Next, the dataset was divided into training and testing groups. Notably, our proposed model demonstrated exceptional performance, with an identification accuracy of 96.7% when compared to other methods such as ResNet3D 95.9% and UNet 94.3%. Additionally, we believe that multi-task learning techniques could also enhance the model's accuracy by incorporating additional clinical data. The non-linear response of the light-matter system amplifies the influence of quantum noise, leading to the collapse of the polariton states. This phenomenon is characterized by a polariton spontaneous emission noise that manifests as a diffusive process in the system's dynamics. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices may hold the capability to achieve a break-through in solving the full separability problem in quantum states, particularly when handling multi-partite states. This capability stems from their capability to execute $BQCP$, a broad family of quantum information protocols that involve repeated preparation of states, followed by measurement and adaptation, within an iterative framework. This particular $BQCP$ family is grounded in the principle that a mixed state with a positive partial transpose is separable if it can be generated from the zero state through anti-commutative interactions applied to an entangled state. We outline a simplified version of an efficient algorithm for separability that is optimized for NISQ devices. This method is specifically tailored for two-qubit states that possess a partial transpose positive property. This approach involves a single use of an anti-correlated entanglement source, followed by measurements on each constituent qubit. We establish that a state can be definitely separable if it meets two specific criteria based on the measurement outcomes of these qubits. This method is currently applicable to a two-qubit system, but it has the potential to be expanded to larger, multipartite states like GHZ states. This method requires an NISQ device to generate an $n$-partite state to demonstrate separability by observing a single event, facilitated by an all-in-one use of an $\textit{ISQ}$ gate that creates an anti-correlated state within the quantum memory. This method has the potential to be optimized and applied to specific families of multipartite states that are currently unknown. This method may also contribute to the development of a quantum machine learning system that facilitates classification of quantum states, leading to applications in solving complex problems in science and society. This research introduces a novel application of self-supervised learning for the task of fashion instance-level image retrieval (FIR). Utilizing a pre-trained model, the research reformulates the problem as a self-supervised learning framework for clothing items. Building upon the idea of contrastive learning, the proposed framework seeks similar items by minimizing the distance between their positive pairs and maximizing the distance between their negative pairs. A new outfit-driven metric learning objective is formulated to capture outfit-level characteristics. To bridge the gap between appearance and structure, the proposed method incorporates a novel structural contrastive learning objective. This approach enhances the robustness of the model by incorporating a feature refinement module that combines appearance and structural features. As a result, the proposed method achieves improved performance on FIR datasets such as the Amazon-ComputingFashion and the DesignGallery datasets, with specific accuracy rates of 83.29 and 67.73 respectively at rank 20. Notably, the research establishes that self-supervised learning can be effective for FIR despite the need for extensive computational resources to achieve top results. Our focus is on the impact of different stopping times, either based on data-driven rules or a predetermined criterion, for two classic problems without a solution: inverse problems and existence-less equations. Like early adoption of gradient descent for problems without a potential, our approach involves analyzing the approximated solution path rather than its actual value. This path is seen as a limiting object under a specific current, defined by a balanced relationship between a distance term and a non-negative, locally-Lipschitz function. We also investigate ways to validate approximated solution paths by finding two functions, one containing the solution path and the other excluding it, such that their intersection is the solution path. In the case of an existence-less problem, these functions are defined by the current's distance and non-negative value, while for an inverse problem without a solution, these functions are characterized by the squared distance and non-negative value, with the solution being their intersection. We established a key relationship by which the solution is the equilibrium point of a new, consistent current, defined as the product of three components: the original current, a data-driven stop-time function, and a discontinuous inverse function. This relationship led to the development of a novel, consistent gradient-like method, where the solution is its limit point. This method, called Disinc, doesn't require inversion and uses the solution of a new, consistent current for its limit point. This method, Disinc, is based on alternating between finding the solution under a current defined by the product of three components and projecting onto a set related to data and inverse function. A new cost constructor for stereo matching has been developed by our team, addressing key challenges associated with this task. These challenges include handling missing pixel values caused by occlusions, reducing noise from these occlusions, and accurately predicting textureless areas. To this end, our cost constructor builds on the GeorgeProp method by integrating a neural network to gauge the reliability of matching costs for each pixel, thereby enabling the direct optimization of occlusion-related issues. Furthermore, instead of geodesic propagation, costs are constructed by iteratively refining pixel-to-pixel similarities on a hierarchical image pyramid. This approach allows us for the first time to leverage the hierarchical representation for direct cost optimization. As a result, our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods on public datasets, including KITTI and Middlebury. Notably, our technique demonstrates notable improvements on KITTI by achieving a 0.5 mm disparity estimation error for occluded pixels, while substantially reducing textureless area errors by as low as 12% when compared to other top-performing methods. A comprehensive analysis and ablation study of our technique are also provided in the supporting repository. This paper introduces a novel approach for associating with access points in home WiFi networks. Unlike the current practice of relying solely on RSSI values to minimize power consumption, our approach leverages the characteristics of different modulations and multiplexing techniques to associate with the optimal access point based on network load and channel conditions. We implement this association mechanism in an iOS device using the iWiFi tool, and assess its performance in a real-world setting involving 9 devices, 7 access points, and 16 humans. Our findings demonstrate that compared to association based solely on signal strength, our method enhances overall network throughput by 30.64%, decreases delay by 50.23%, and decreases power consumption by 26.67%. Furthermore, our results reveal that this optimization technique not only benefits the device itself but also improves the overall network performance for other connected devices. Finally, our work highlights the practical difficulties of implementing optimized WiFi behavior, including device limitations and user behavior, and their implications for research and practice. The source code of our association mechanism is publicly available at https://github.com/UniversiteLIRIS/ChannelLoadAssociation.
